tool.name: Google Analytics
tool.tagline: Measure how people find and use your website with Google Analytics 4
tool.description: Google Analytics 4 (GA4) is Google's free web and app analytics product. A small tag on your site sends events to a property, and GA4 turns them into reports about traffic sources, engagement, conversions and revenue, plus the Explore workspace for ad-hoc analysis. Learning it well means knowing the event data model, instrumenting a site correctly, and reading and building the right reports and explorations.

Google's free web analytics tool. A small piece of code on your pages sends records of what visitors do, and GA4 turns them into reports.
The previous version of Google Analytics, which stopped collecting data in July 2023. Its terms, like goals and hit types, don't apply to GA4.
The paid version of Google Analytics for very large sites, with higher limits than the free version.

.)

When a visitor does what the site hoped for, such as buying or signing up. GA4 now calls the events that count as conversions key events.

concepts.name: What Google Analytics 4 is
concepts.summary: GA4 is Google's free tool for measuring how people use a website or app; it records each visitor action as an event.
concepts.why: Knowing what GA4 measures and how it differs from the old product tells you what its numbers mean.
concepts.body:
Imagine running a shop and wanting to know how many people came in, which door they used, what they looked at and what they bought. **Web analytics** is the same idea for a website: measuring what visitors do, so you can improve the site. **Google Analytics 4** (GA4) is Google's free web analytics tool, and the most widely used one.

It works like this. You add a small piece of code from Google, called a **tag**, to every page of your site (apps use a code kit from Google instead). Each time a visitor does something, such as opening a page, scrolling, clicking a download link or buying, the tag sends a short message about it to Google. Each of those messages is an **event**.

GA4 collects the events and turns them into reports: tables and charts showing how many people visited, where they came from (a Google search, an email, an ad), what they did, and whether they **converted**, that is, did what you hoped for, like signing up or buying.

GA4 replaced the older **Universal Analytics** (UA), which stopped collecting data in July 2023. Much of what you read online still describes UA, with words like "goals" and "hit types". Those don't apply to GA4:

- Everything is an event. A page being opened is simply an event named `page_view`.
- Each event carries details, such as which page it was or how much was paid.
- GA4 is built around people and what they do, and can combine a website and its phone app in one place.

There are two ways to look at the data: ready-made **standard reports** for everyday questions, and the **Explore** workspace for building your own one-off analyses.

GA4 is free for most sites. A paid version, **Analytics 360**, raises the limits for very large sites; this course covers the free version unless it says otherwise.

People use GA4 to answer questions like: which ad campaigns bring buyers, which pages make people leave, where people give up in a sign-up form, and how many of last month's new visitors came back.
takeaways: GA4 is event-based: every visitor action, including opening a page, is an event
Universal Analytics stopped in July 2023; its words (goals, hit types) don't apply to GA4
Two ways to look at data: standard reports and Explore

quiz.q: How does GA4 record a page view?
options: As a page_view event with parameters
As a special pageview hit type
Only in Realtime, not in reports
quiz.explain: GA4 has one kind of data, the event; a page view is the page_view event, with details such as the page's address (page_location).

concepts.name: Accounts, properties and data streams
concepts.summary: An account holds properties; a property holds data streams; a website's data stream gives you the G- measurement ID.
concepts.why: You cannot install or administer GA4 without knowing which of the three layers a setting lives on.
concepts.body:
Before any data arrives, you set up three levels in GA4, one inside the other, like a filing cabinet, its drawers and the folders in each drawer.

- An **account** is the top level, usually one per company. It holds company-wide settings, such as who has access and whether data is shared with Google.
- A **property** is where data is stored and reports are built. Usually there is one per business or product, and it can combine a website with its phone apps. Most settings live here: time zone, currency, how long data is kept, and the settings later lessons cover.
- A **data stream** is one source of data flowing into a property: a web stream for a website, or an app stream for an iOS or Android app. Each web stream has a **measurement ID** that looks like `G-ABC123XYZ`. The tag on your pages sends its events to that ID, like the address on an envelope.

A common mistake is creating one property per section of a website, or per country, and then wanting to compare them. One report can't combine two properties. Use a single property instead, and split the data inside its reports by website address, page or country.

The **Admin** area (the gear icon, bottom left) has two columns, Account and Property. In the Property column you'll mostly use three groups:

- *Data collection and modification*: data streams, which visits to leave out, how long data is kept, deletion requests;
- *Data display*: settings for events and the other features later lessons cover;
- *Product links*: connections to other Google products, such as Google's advertising service.

Each web stream also has **Configure tag settings**, for finer control of the tag: for example, how many minutes without activity end a visit, and which visits come from your own staff.
takeaways: Account > property > data stream; the web stream's G- ID is what you install
One property per business, not per section of a site; split the data inside reports instead
Admin is organised into Account and Property columns

quiz.q: Where do you set how long GA4 keeps its data?
quiz.explain: How long data is kept, like most data settings, belongs to the property.

quiz.q: What does a measurement ID like G-ABC123XYZ identify?
quiz.explain: Each web data stream has its own G- measurement ID; app streams use their own app IDs.

concepts.name: Events and parameters
concepts.summary: Every visitor action is an event with a name and parameters that describe it; GA4 has four kinds of events.
concepts.why: The event model is the foundation of every report, analysis and custom setting you will ever build.
concepts.body:
In GA4 an **event** is a record of one thing a visitor did, with a name: `page_view` (opened a page), `scroll`, `purchase`, `sign_up`. Names are written in lower case with underscores between words, a style called **snake_case**.

Each event also carries **parameters**: extra details, each one a name with a value, like labels on a parcel. A `purchase` event might carry `value: 49` and `currency: "EUR"`; a `page_view` carries `page_location`, the page's URL. Some parameters are added to every event automatically, such as the page title and the visitor's language; others you send yourself.

Events come from four places, from least to most work:

- **Automatically collected**: sent by the tag with no setup, such as `first_visit` (someone's first visit), `session_start` (a visit begins) and `user_engagement` (the page was in use).
- **Enhanced measurement**: extra actions you switch on in the data stream's settings, such as `scroll`, clicks on links to other websites, `file_download` and `video_start`.
- **Recommended**: events Google has named and documented, with the parameters they should carry: `login`, `sign_up`, `purchase`, `generate_lead` (someone sent a contact form). Using these exact names makes ready-made reports work.
- **Custom**: any other event you name yourself, like `newsletter_toggle`.

Limits to remember: event names can be up to 40 characters, and capitals matter, so `Sign_Up` and `sign_up` are two different events. An event can carry up to 25 parameters of your own, and each value can be up to 100 characters. Anything over a limit is silently dropped.

Reports only show the parameters GA4 knows about. The standard ones are built in. Your own must be registered as a **custom dimension** (for text, like a plan name) or a **custom metric** (for numbers); a later lesson shows how. Until then they are still collected, and you can see them in DebugView, GA4's live event viewer.

Standard reports show events added up into totals; Explore can work with the individual events.
takeaways: Event = name + parameters; parameters describe the event
Automatic, enhanced measurement, recommended, custom: in that order of effort
Your own parameters need a custom dimension or metric to appear in reports

quiz.q: You send a custom parameter plan_type with your sign_up event. Where will you see it immediately?
options: In the Events report as a column
In DebugView, but not in standard reports until registered
Nowhere until you create an audience
quiz.explain: Parameters you haven't registered are collected but only show in DebugView; a custom dimension makes them appear in reports.

quiz.q: Which event category requires no configuration at all?
quiz.explain: first_visit, session_start and user_engagement are sent by the tag with no settings.

concepts.name: Users, sessions and engagement
concepts.summary: How GA4 counts visitors and visits (sessions), and what makes a visit or a visitor 'engaged'.
concepts.why: Engagement rate replaced bounce rate as the main measure of visit quality, and 'users' in GA4 reports means active users.
concepts.body:
GA4 counts people and visits. To tell people apart, the tag stores a random ID in a **cookie**: a small piece of text a website saves in your browser so it can recognise the browser next time. GA4's cookie is called `_ga`. The ID isn't a name; it only says "same browser as before". Sites where people log in can also send their own user ID (see the Reporting identity lesson).

GA4 reports three counts of users:

- *Total users*: everyone who did anything.
- *New users*: people on their first visit (they triggered `first_visit`).
- *Active users*: people who had an engaged visit (explained below) or their first visit in the period. Plain "Users" in reports means **active users**.

A **session** is one visit. It starts with the automatic `session_start` event and ends after 30 minutes with no activity. You can change that timeout to anything from 5 minutes to almost 8 hours in the web stream's tag settings. Every event carries a session ID parameter, `ga_session_id`, so GA4 knows which visit it belongs to.

Unlike Universal Analytics, a GA4 session doesn't restart at midnight, or when a visitor comes back through a different ad. So GA4 usually shows fewer sessions than UA did for the same site.

A session is **engaged** when at least one of these is true:

- it lasted longer than 10 seconds (you can raise this to 60 seconds),
- it included a key event: an event you've marked as a success, such as a purchase (a later lesson),
- it had two or more page views.

A **metric** is a number GA4 calculates, like *Sessions* or *Users*. The main engagement metrics are:

- **Engagement rate** = engaged sessions ÷ all sessions.
- **Bounce rate**: the opposite share, 1 minus the engagement rate.
- *Average engagement time*: how long the page was actually on screen, measured by the `user_engagement` event. Time in a background tab doesn't count.
- *Views per session* and *Sessions per user*.

Because the tag measures time in the browser, someone who reads one page for 2 minutes and leaves counts as engaged. Universal Analytics would have called that a bounce.
takeaways: "Users" in reports means active users, not total users
Sessions end after 30 minutes without activity and don't split at midnight
Engaged session: over 10 s, or a key event, or 2+ page views; engagement rate is the main measure

quiz.q: A visitor reads one page for 45 seconds and leaves. In GA4 the session is...
options: A bounce, since only one page was viewed
Engaged, because it lasted more than 10 seconds
Engaged only if a key event fired
quiz.explain: Any session over 10 seconds counts as engaged regardless of page count.

concepts.name: Dimensions, metrics and scope
concepts.summary: Dimensions describe, metrics count, and each belongs to a user, session, event or item scope.
concepts.why: Mixing scopes is the most common reason a GA4 table looks wrong or shows (not set).
concepts.body:
Every GA4 table has two kinds of column. **Dimensions** are descriptions, usually text: country, page path (the part of a URL after the domain, like `/pricing`), event name, the source a visit came from. **Metrics** are numbers: users, sessions, event count, revenue.

Dimensions decide the rows, and metrics fill in the numbers. "Sessions by country" has one row per country, with a count of sessions in each.

Each dimension and metric has a **scope**: the thing it describes. There are four:

- **User** scope: the person, such as *First user source* (how they first found you), *Age* and *Lifetime value* (all the money they've spent).
- **Session** scope: one visit, such as *Session source / medium* (where this visit came from), *Landing page* (the first page of the visit) and the metric *Sessions*.
- **Event** scope: a single event, such as *Event name*, *Page location* and *Link URL*, and the metric *Event count*. Most custom dimensions are event-scoped.
- **Item** scope: one product inside a shop event, such as *Item name*, *Item brand* and *Item revenue*. Shop events carry a list of the products involved (see the ecommerce lessons).

You can mix scopes, but not every mix makes sense. *Sessions* by *Event name* asks "how many sessions included each event", which is fine. The count of `purchase` events by *Landing page* is also fine, because each purchase happened during a session, and that session had one landing page.

Other mixes don't line up one to one. A user has many sessions; one purchase event can include many items. So a session dimension with a user metric, or an item dimension with an event metric, gives `(not set)` rows or numbers that are too big.

A practical rule: start from the metric you want, then only add dimensions of the same scope or a wider one (an event sits inside a session, which belongs to a user). In Explore the dimension picker marks combinations that don't fit, and standard reports simply won't add them.

`(not set)` in a row usually means the dimension had no value for those events, not that data was lost.
takeaways: Dimensions describe, metrics count; both have a scope
Scopes: user, session, event, item
Add dimensions of the same or a wider scope than your metric to avoid (not set)

quiz.q: Which pairing is most likely to produce a misleading table?
quiz.explain: Item dimensions describe products inside shop events; one visit can involve many products, so they don't line up with a count of sessions.

concepts.name: Reporting identity
concepts.summary: How GA4 decides that two events belong to the same person: User-ID, device ID and estimates.
concepts.why: Changing the identity setting silently changes your user counts and can make GA4 hide small rows for privacy.
concepts.body:
GA4 can recognise a person in several ways, called **identity spaces**. Each is a kind of ID:

- **User-ID**: your own ID for a customer, which you send (`user_id` in the config or an event) when someone is logged in. It is the only space that joins the same person across browsers and devices.
- **Device ID**: the random ID in the `_ga` cookie on the web, called the **client ID**, or the app-instance ID in apps. The default when nothing else is available.
- **Modelled data**: when people refuse cookies in a cookie banner (see the consent mode lesson), GA4 can estimate what they did from the behaviour of people who accepted. Such estimates are called **modelling**.

Until February 2024 **Google signals** (Google's data about people signed in to a Google account who allow personalised ads) was also an identity space. It no longer is. Google signals still provides age, gender and interests, and lists of past visitors to show ads to, but it no longer joins a person's devices together in reports.

In Admin > Reporting identity you pick how these spaces are combined:

- **Blended**: User-ID, then device ID, then modelled data. Default.
- **Observed**: User-ID, then device ID. No modelling.
- **Device-based**: device ID only; ignores User-ID.

The choice affects reports only, not collection, so you can switch back and forth: nothing is lost. Why switch? Because when an identity space could reveal individuals, GA4 applies **data thresholding**: it hides rows that represent only a few people. If you see the thresholding warning icon in a report and need the full rows, temporarily switch to Device-based.

A User-ID must not reveal who the person is (no email addresses), must be exactly the same text everywhere, and user counts fall when you add it because cross-device duplicates collapse. That drop is correct, not an error.
takeaways: Identity spaces: User-ID, device ID, modelled; Google signals left identity in 2024
Blended / Observed / Device-based are report-time settings, reversible
Thresholding (hidden small rows) is tied to identity; Device-based avoids it

quiz.q: You switch Reporting identity from Blended to Device-based. What happens to already-collected data?
options: Nothing; only how reports join events changes
It is reprocessed and duplicates are removed for good
Events without a User-ID are deleted
quiz.explain: Reporting identity is applied each time a report is built, so switching changes nothing stored.

quiz.q: Which identity space can join the same person on a phone and a laptop?
quiz.explain: Only an ID you set when the person logs in survives across devices.

concepts.name: Installing the tag with gtag.js
concepts.summary: Paste the Google tag snippet into <head> on every page, or load GA4 through Google Tag Manager.
concepts.why: No tag, no data: this is the first thing you do on any site, and it decides where every later change happens.
concepts.body:
The simplest install is the **Google tag** snippet: a few lines of HTML you copy from Admin > Data streams > your web stream > *View tag instructions*. It already contains your measurement ID. Put it as high in the `<head>` as you can, on every page, error pages included, so every visit is counted the same way.

The snippet loads Google's script, `gtag.js`, with `async`, so it downloads without holding up the page. Then it sets things up in three steps, which you can see in the example:

- `window.dataLayer = ...` creates the **data layer**: a list in the page where messages for Google wait until the script is ready.
- `function gtag(){...}` creates `gtag()`, the command you use to talk to GA4. Every call adds a message to the data layer.
- `gtag('config', 'G-...')` connects the page to your data stream. It sends the first `page_view` event and sets the `_ga` cookie, a small piece of text saved in the browser to recognise it on the next visit.

Optional settings go in curly braces after the ID: `send_page_view: false` stops the automatic page view (when you send your own), `user_id` passes the ID of a logged-in user, and `debug_mode: true` makes your events show in DebugView.

The alternative is **Google Tag Manager** (GTM), a free Google tool for managing all of a site's tags in one place. You put one GTM snippet on the site, then add the Google tag and any GA4 event tags inside GTM's website, by pointing and clicking. GTM is the better choice when marketers need to add or change tags without asking developers to change the site, or when a site uses many tracking tools. The plain snippet suits a small site, or one that developers fully control. Never use both for the same measurement ID, or every page view is counted twice.

Website builders such as WordPress, Shopify and Wix usually offer an add-on, a **plugin**, that inserts the same snippet for you. What matters is that exactly one tag with your G- ID runs on each page.

After installing, open the Realtime report or DebugView and load your page: you should see yourself within seconds. Full reports take 24 to 48 hours to fill in.
concepts.code: Welcome
takeaways: One Google tag snippet in <head> on every page, or one Google Tag Manager snippet
gtag('config', ...) fires the first page_view and accepts options
Never run gtag.js and a GTM Google tag for the same ID together
pitfalls: Installing the snippet twice (theme + plugin) and doubling every page view.

quiz.q: Why is the Google tag placed in <head> rather than at the end of <body>?
options: So page_view fires early and consistently before the user leaves
It would not work in body
head is required by HTML for scripts
It makes the page load faster
quiz.explain: The script loads without holding up the page (async), and starting early catches even very short visits.

concepts.name: Enhanced measurement
concepts.summary: Switch on automatic scroll, outbound click, site search, video, file download and form events in the web data stream.
concepts.why: It gives you most of the interaction events a marketing site needs without writing any code.
concepts.body:
**Enhanced measurement** is a set of switches in your web data stream's settings (Admin > Data streams > your data stream). When they're on, the tag watches what happens in the browser and sends events for you, with no code:

- **Page views** (`page_view`), with an option to count a new page view whenever the address changes without a new page loading. Some sites, called **single-page applications**, swap their content in place like that instead of loading new pages (see the Expert lesson on them).
- **Scrolls** (`scroll`): once per page, when the visitor reaches 90% of the way down. There's no 25/50/75% option; that needs GTM or your own code.
- **Outbound clicks** (`click` with `link_url` and `outbound: true`): clicks on links to other websites. Your own other sites, once listed for cross-domain tracking, don't count as outbound.
- **Site search** (`view_search_results` with `search_term`): sent when a page's URL has a search word in its query string, such as `?q=shoes`. GA4 looks for `q`, `s`, `search`, `query` or `keyword`, and you can add your own.
- **Form interactions** (`form_start`, `form_submit`), with `form_id`, `form_name` and `form_destination`.
- **Video engagement** (`video_start`, `video_progress`, `video_complete`) for embedded YouTube videos whose embed URL allows JavaScript control (`enablejsapi=1`).
- **File downloads** (`file_download`) for links to common document, archive, audio and video files, such as `.pdf`, `.zip` or `.mp3`.

GA4 already knows these events and their parameters, so they appear in reports without custom dimensions. They count toward the same limits as any other event.

Switch off what you don't need. Form interactions are the usual problem. If the page header has a search box or a newsletter form, `form_start` fires on nearly every page and clutters reports. And on sites whose forms are run by JavaScript, `form_submit` can fire when nothing was really sent. Video events only work for YouTube, not Vimeo or the HTML `<video>` element.

Enhanced measurement is a good first layer; your own events for sign-ups and purchases go on top of it.
takeaways: Seven switches on the web stream give you interaction events with no code
Scroll fires only at 90%; video works only for YouTube embeds
Disable noisy switches (often form interactions) rather than filtering later
pitfalls: Expecting video events from Vimeo or a native <video> element; only YouTube embeds are supported.

quiz.q: A user scrolls to 50% of a page. Which enhanced measurement event fires?
quiz.explain: The built-in scroll event has a single 90% threshold; finer tracking needs GTM or custom code.

concepts.name: Sending custom events with gtag
concepts.summary: Use gtag('event', name, {params}) to record interactions GA4 cannot see on its own, preferring recommended names.
concepts.why: Sign-ups, leads, feature usage and anything business-specific must be sent by you.
concepts.body:
Anything that is not a page view, scroll or click needs an explicit call:

```javascript
gtag('event', 'sign_up', { method: 'email' });
```

The first value is the event name, the second the parameters, in curly braces. Before inventing a name, check the **recommended events** list (`login`, `sign_up`, `search`, `share`, `generate_lead`, `select_content`, `tutorial_begin`, and the ecommerce set). Recommended names are not magic in themselves, but GA4 and Google Ads know their expected parameters, ready-made reports pick them up, and GA4's forecasts of who will buy (predictive metrics, an Advanced lesson) rely on `purchase` specifically.

Rules for names and parameters:

- snake_case, letters/digits/underscores, max 40 characters, case-sensitive (`Sign_Up` and `sign_up` are two events).
- Do not prefix with `google_`, `ga_` or `firebase_`; those are reserved.
- Up to 25 custom parameters per event; values up to 100 characters; send numbers as numbers (`3`, not `'3'` in quotes) if you will make a metric of them.
- Keep **cardinality**, the number of different values a parameter has, reasonable. A parameter like `search_term` is fine; one holding full URLs full of unique codes creates millions of different values, and reports then lump most of them into one `(other)` row.

Where to fire the event: on the action that means something, usually the *success* of a form (after the server answers), not the button click. In the example, `addEventListener('submit', ...)` runs the code that follows whenever the form is sent; `fetch` sends the form to the server, and the event goes to GA4 only if the server answers OK (`res.ok`). Keep this code in your JavaScript files rather than in `onclick` attributes in the HTML, so the tracking lives in one place.

If you use GTM, the equivalent is adding a message to the data layer and letting a GA4 event tag in GTM read it; the event naming rules are identical.
takeaways: gtag('event', name, params) is how you record business interactions
Prefer recommended event names; custom names are fine when nothing fits
Fire on success, keep names consistent, avoid parameters with huge numbers of different values

quiz.q: Which event name will GA4 treat as a different event from sign_up?
quiz.explain: Event names are case-sensitive, so inconsistent casing splits your data.

quiz.q: Where should a 'form submitted' event usually fire?
quiz.explain: Firing on success avoids counting validation failures and double clicks as conversions.

concepts.name: Key events (conversions)
concepts.summary: Mark the events that represent success as key events so GA4 counts and attributes them everywhere.
concepts.why: Key events drive the key-event reports, attribution, Google Ads bidding and engaged-session logic.
concepts.body:
A **key event** is an event you have flagged as important: a purchase, a lead form, a sign-up. Until March 2024 GA4 called these *conversions*; the rename happened so that "conversion" means the same thing in Google Ads (an ad-driven key event). Older articles and Google Ads' own screens still say conversions.

Marking one is a toggle, not code. In Admin > Events (or Admin > Key events) find the event name and switch **Mark as key event**. If the event has not been seen yet, create the key event by name in advance; it activates when the first one arrives. The flag is not retroactive: events from before you switched it on are not counted as key events.

You can have up to 30 key events per property (50 in 360). Each has a **counting method**: *once per event* (default, right for purchases) or *once per session* (right for leads, where one person submitting twice is still one lead).

Once flagged, the event appears in the *Key events* report, in acquisition reports as *Key events* and *Session key event rate*, in Explore as a metric, in the Advertising section's reports on which channels earned the credit, and, if you link Google Ads, in Google Ads as a conversion it can import. A session with a key event also counts as engaged.

A frequent mistake is marking `page_view` with a URL condition. GA4 cannot do that directly; instead, create a new event in Admin > Events > *Create event* that fires when `page_view` has `page_location` containing `/thank-you`, then mark that derived event as key. Better still, send an explicit `generate_lead` event from the form.
takeaways: Key event = flagged event; 'conversion' is the old name and the Google Ads name
Toggle in Admin, max 30 per property, not retroactive
Counting method: once per event (purchases) vs once per session (leads)

quiz.q: A lead form can be submitted twice in one visit. Which counting method avoids double-counting?
quiz.explain: Once per session counts the key event at most once per session regardless of repeats.

concepts.name: User properties and custom definitions
concepts.summary: Register your own parameters as custom dimensions and metrics, and describe users with user properties.
concepts.why: Without registration your parameters are collected but invisible in reports and explorations.
concepts.body:
GA4 only puts a parameter in the dimension picker once you tell it to. Admin > Custom definitions is where you do that.

A **custom dimension** maps a parameter name to a reportable dimension and has a scope:

- *Event-scoped*: the parameter is on an event (`billing_period`, `article_author`). Up to 50 per property.
- *User-scoped*: a **user property**, an attribute of the person (`plan`, `account_type`). Up to 25.
- *Item-scoped*: your own detail on each product in an ecommerce `items` list (`item_colour`). Up to 10.

A **custom metric** maps a numeric parameter to a metric (`plan_count`, `video_seconds`) with a unit (standard, currency, distance, time). Up to 50.

User properties are sent separately from events with `gtag('set', 'user_properties', {...})` before the events they should describe; GA4 attaches the latest value to every subsequent event from that user, and reports show the value in effect at the time of each event. They are ideal for things that change rarely: subscription plan, the month someone signed up, preferred language. Never put personal data (name, email) in them.

Registration is not retroactive. Data for a custom dimension starts from the moment you create it, even though the parameter was collected earlier; Only the BigQuery export (an Advanced lesson) keeps the earlier raw values. Create definitions on the same day you start sending the parameter, and you can't delete a definition, only archive (hide) it, so name carefully.

Dimensions with huge numbers of different values (unique IDs, exact times, long free text) burst the row limits and end up as `(other)`. Keep values to a small set of repeating categories.
takeaways: Custom dimensions: event (50), user (25), item (10); custom metrics: 50
User properties describe the person and ride along on every later event
Registration is not retroactive; avoid values that are nearly all different

quiz.q: You started sending a parameter two weeks ago and register a custom dimension today. In standard reports it shows data from...
options: Only after 48 hours, then from two weeks ago
quiz.explain: Custom definitions fill in from the moment you create them; only the BigQuery export has the earlier raw values.

concepts.name: Verifying with DebugView and Realtime
concepts.summary: Check that events and parameters arrive as intended before you trust a single report.
concepts.why: Reports take a day or more to fill in, so DebugView and Realtime are the only quick way to check your tracking.
concepts.body:
After any change to your tracking, check it live instead of waiting a day or two for the reports. GA4 gives you two tools.

**Realtime** (Reports > Realtime) shows activity from the last 30 minutes: visitors by page, event names, key events and where visitors came from. It's enough to confirm that the tag loads and the main events arrive. But it shows no parameters, and your visit is mixed in with everyone else's.

**DebugView** (Admin > DebugView) shows the events from one browser at a time, second by second, with every parameter, and whether each event counts as a key event (an event marked as a success, from a later lesson). A browser appears there only when its events carry the `debug_mode` parameter. Three ways to switch it on:

- add `debug_mode: true` to the `gtag('config', ...)` call on a **staging** site, a test copy of your site that real visitors don't see;
- install the *Google Analytics Debugger* extension for Chrome, which switches it on for every site you visit;
- use **Tag Assistant** (tagassistant.google.com), Google's checking tool for tags, in preview mode.

Tag Assistant also shows, for each tag, what made it fire or not, and the exact message it sent. That makes it the best tool when the question is "why didn't this tag fire?".

The final word belongs to the browser's own developer tools (right-click the page and choose Inspect). Their Network panel lists every request the page makes. Type `collect?` in its filter box, and each GA4 request appears, with all its parameters in its query string.

A checking routine: load the page in a private window and expect `page_view`, `session_start` and `first_visit`. Do the action and expect your event, with the right parameters and with numbers sent as numbers. Check that nothing arrives twice, and that the key event flag is set. Then wait 24 to 48 hours and confirm the event appears in the Events report.
takeaways: Realtime: last 30 minutes, everyone, no parameters
DebugView: one browser, every parameter, needs debug_mode
Tag Assistant / Network tab answer 'why did it not fire'

quiz.q: You see your custom event in DebugView but its parameter value is missing. Most likely cause?
options: The parameter name has a typo, or its value was empty when the gtag call ran
The event is not a key event
quiz.explain: DebugView shows all parameters that arrive; if one is absent, the tag did not send it.

concepts.name: UTM parameters and campaign tracking
concepts.summary: Tag your campaign URLs with utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign so GA4 attributes traffic correctly.
concepts.why: Without UTMs, email, social and paid visits are counted as Direct or Referral, and your acquisition reports are wrong.
concepts.body:
When a visit starts, GA4 works out where the visitor came from. It has three clues:

- the **referrer**: the address of the page the visitor clicked through from, which the browser passes along (for example, a Google results page);
- `gclid`, a parameter Google Ads adds to its ad links automatically (**auto-tagging**);
- **UTM parameters** that you add to the end of your own links.

UTM parameters go in the link's query string, the part after `?`. Use them on every link you control that brings people to your site from somewhere else: newsletters, social posts, ads on other platforms.

- `utm_source`: who sent the visitor, e.g. `newsletter`, `facebook`, `partner-blog`.
- `utm_medium`: the kind of channel, e.g. `email`, `cpc` (ads paid per click), `social`, `affiliate`. GA4 uses this value to sort visits into channels like Email or Paid Search, so use the standard spellings.
- `utm_campaign`: the campaign name, e.g. `spring_sale_2026`.
- `utm_term` and `utm_content`: the search keyword, and which version of the ad or link; both optional.
- `utm_id` and a few newer ones, used mainly when importing campaign data into GA4; you can ignore them at first.

Values are case-sensitive: `Email` and `email` become two separate rows. Agree on one naming style (lower case, hyphens or underscores, no spaces) and keep a shared spreadsheet of campaign names. Google's *Campaign URL Builder* page writes correct links for you.

In reports the values appear as *Session source*, *Session medium* and *Session campaign*, which describe each visit, and as *First user source* and so on, which describe how the person arrived the very first time.

GA4's **default channel group** turns these values into channels: `email` becomes Email; `cpc`, `ppc` or `paidsearch` become Paid Search; `social` from a known social network becomes Organic Social.

Never put UTMs on links between pages of your own site: clicking one gives the visit a new source halfway through. And don't add your own UTMs to Google Ads links when auto-tagging is on; `gclid` carries far more detail.
concepts.code: Shop the sale Shop now Bad
takeaways: utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign on every link you control
utm_medium decides the channel group; use standard values like email, cpc, social
Case-sensitive; never on links between your own pages

quiz.q: Which utm_medium value makes a session fall into the Email channel?
quiz.explain: The default channel group matches the medium against a fixed list; it needs 'email' (or 'e-mail', 'e_mail', 'e mail').

concepts.name: Single-page apps and cross-domain tracking
concepts.summary: Handle sites that change pages without reloading, and journeys across several domains, so sessions and page views stay correct.
concepts.why: These two setups are where most broken GA4 implementations live: doubled page views, self-referrals and split sessions.
concepts.body:
**Single-page applications** change the address with the History API, the browser's feature for updating the URL without loading a new page. So the Google tag's first `page_view` fires once, and then never again. Two fixes:

- Enhanced measurement's *Page changes based on browser history events* fires `page_view` on `pushState`/`replaceState`/`popstate`. It is easy but naive: it fires on query-string-only changes, and `page_title` is read straight away, before your app has updated `<title>`.
- Set `send_page_view: false` in the config and send `page_view` yourself from the **router** (the part of the app that switches views) once each view has changed and its title and content are ready. Send `page_location`, `page_title` and `page_referrer` explicitly; the referrer must be the previous virtual page, not `document.referrer`, or every view appears to come from the entry page.

Never do both or every route change is counted twice.

**Cross-domain tracking** is needed when one journey spans domains (`example.com` to `checkout.example-pay.com`). Cookies are per domain, so the second domain would start a new user and a new session whose source is the first domain: a *self-referral*. Fix it in Admin > Data streams > stream > Configure tag settings > **Configure your domains**: list every domain. The tag then appends a `_gl` linker parameter to links and form posts between those domains, and the receiving page reads it to keep the same client ID (the `_ga` cookie's ID) and session.

Checklist for cross-domain: all domains in the list, the same measurement ID on all of them, links are real `<a>`/`<form>` elements (for navigation done by JavaScript, read the client ID with `gtag('get', ...)` and add `_gl` yourself), and the second domain is also in *List unwanted referrals* so it never counts as a source. Subdomains of one domain (`shop.example.com` and `blog.example.com`) share cookies and need none of this.
takeaways: SPA: either the history-change switch or manual page_view with send_page_view:false, never both
Send page_referrer as the previous virtual page
Cross-domain: list all domains in tag settings; the _gl linker carries the client ID
pitfalls: Keeping the enhanced-measurement history switch on while also sending page_view manually.

quiz.q: After enabling cross-domain tracking, sessions from checkout.example-pay.com still show source example.com. What did you forget?
options: To add the second domain to the unwanted referrals list
quiz.explain: The linker joins the user; unwanted referrals stops the first domain being recorded as the session's referrer.

quiz.q: In an SPA with manual page_view events, what should page_referrer be?
quiz.explain: Using document.referrer would attribute every virtual view to the external entry referrer.

concepts.name: Reports snapshot, date ranges and comparisons
concepts.summary: Find your way around the Reports section: snapshot, Realtime, collections, dates, comparisons and filters.
concepts.why: Every report shares the same controls; learning them once makes all of GA4 readable.
concepts.body:
The **Reports** section (in the menu on the left) opens on the *Reports snapshot*. It's a **dashboard**: one page of summary cards, showing users, sessions, top channels, top pages and key events, plus *Insights*, unusual changes GA4 spotted by itself.

Below it come Realtime and then the **collections**, groups of related reports:

- *Life cycle*: Acquisition (where visitors come from), Engagement (what they do), Monetization (what they buy) and Retention (whether they come back).
- *User*: who the visitors are (User attributes) and what devices and browsers they use (Tech).
- Newer properties may show collections built around a business goal instead, such as *Generate leads* or *Drive online sales*.

Each collection has *overview* reports made of cards, and *detail* reports with a chart above a table.

The controls at the top work the same in every report:

- **Date range**: ready-made ranges or your own; tick *Compare* to add an earlier period and get % change columns. Today's data is incomplete, and the last 24 to 48 hours can still change.
- **Comparisons**: up to five conditions side by side, such as *Device category = mobile* against *desktop*. They apply to the whole report and stay on as you move between reports, but not after you reload the page.
- **Add filter** (in the table's toolbar): keeps only the rows matching a condition, such as *Country = Germany*, in this report. It's temporary; you can't save it.
- The **+** next to the table's first column adds a **secondary dimension**: a second breakdown, such as each country split by device.
- The search box above a table keeps only rows containing your text.

Tables list only the top rows (10 to 250 at a time); for the rest, use Explore. The *Share* button downloads a report as a PDF or a CSV file (a simple spreadsheet format), or makes a link to it.

Standard reports count all your data and keep your history for as long as the property exists. Rows representing very few people can still be hidden for privacy, which the Reporting identity lesson explains.
takeaways: Snapshot and Realtime at the top; Life cycle and User collections below
Date range with Compare, up to five comparisons, temporary report filters
Standard reports count all your data, but very small rows can be hidden for privacy

quiz.q: You want mobile vs desktop side by side in the Pages report. What do you use?
quiz.explain: Comparisons show up to five conditions side by side in the same report; a secondary dimension would add rows, not columns.

concepts.name: Acquisition reports and channel groups
concepts.summary: User acquisition vs traffic acquisition, and how source and medium become default channel groups.
concepts.why: Acquisition is the report marketers open first, and the difference between its two versions trips everyone up.
concepts.body:
The **Acquisition** collection answers "where did people come from?". It has two detail reports that look alike and are easy to confuse:

- **User acquisition** uses *user-scoped* dimensions: *First user source*, *First user medium*, *First user default channel group*. They describe how each person arrived the **first time ever**. A visitor who found you through Google a year ago and came back from an email today still counts under Organic Search here.
- **Traffic acquisition** uses *session-scoped* dimensions: *Session source / medium*, *Session default channel group*, *Session campaign*. Each visit is credited to the source that started it, so today's email visit counts as Email.

Use user acquisition to judge which channels bring new people, and traffic acquisition to judge which channels bring visits and results now.

Default channel groups are buckets built by fixed rules from source, medium and campaign: Direct, Organic Search, Paid Search, Organic Social, Paid Social, Email, Referral, Affiliates, Display, Organic Video, Paid Video and a few more. **Unassigned** means the values matched no rule, which almost always means a non-standard `utm_medium`. In Admin you can also define up to two custom channel groups with your own buckets, without changing the default one.

**Direct** means no referrer and no campaign parameters: typed addresses, bookmarks, emails without UTMs, many phone apps, and visits where the browser hid the referrer for privacy. A large Direct share usually means links without UTMs, not loyal fans.

Typical columns are users or sessions, engaged sessions, engagement rate, average engagement time, *Key events* (completed successes such as purchases, which you choose in Admin; see the Key events lesson) and *Session key event rate*, the share of sessions with a key event.
takeaways: User acquisition = first-ever source (user scope); Traffic acquisition = this visit's source
Default channel groups are rule-based buckets from source, medium and campaign
Unassigned and an oversized Direct share point to links with missing or odd UTMs

quiz.q: A user first arrived from Instagram a month ago and buys today after clicking a newsletter link. Which report credits Email?
quiz.explain: Traffic acquisition is session-scoped; user acquisition keeps the first-ever source (Organic Social).

concepts.name: Engagement, retention and user reports
concepts.summary: Read the Events, Pages and screens, Landing page, Retention, User attributes and Tech reports.
concepts.why: These reports answer what people did once they arrived and whether they came back.
concepts.body:
The **Engagement** collection is about what visitors do on the site.

- **Events**: one row per event name, with event count, total users, events per user and revenue. Click an event name to see cards for its parameters. It's the quickest way to confirm that your own events are arriving.
- **Key events**: the same, for just the events you've marked as key events.
- **Pages and screens**: views, users, views per user, average engagement time and key events for each page title. ("Screen" is the app version of a page, which is why the dimension is called `Page title and screen class`.) Pages that share a title are merged into one row, so switch the first column to `Page path and screen class` to get one row per page path.
- **Landing page**: the first page of each visit, with sessions, engagement rate and key events. `(not set)` rows are visits whose first event wasn't a page view, often a new session in a tab left open for a long time.

The **Retention** collection shows new and returning users over time; *user retention* curves (what share of one day's new users came back on day 1, 7 and 30); engagement over time; and *lifetime value*, the revenue each user brings over time. It's based on when people first arrived, so it needs a few weeks of data to be meaningful.

The **User** collection has two reports. **User attributes** shows age, gender and interests, plus language, country and the audiences (saved groups of users) people belong to. Age, gender and interests only appear if you switch on **Google signals**, Google's data about people signed in to a Google account, and only for groups large enough to protect privacy.

**Tech** shows browser, operating system, device category, screen size and app version. It's where to look when one browser shows a strangely low engagement rate, which usually means a JavaScript error in that browser.

Every detail report's table supports a secondary dimension and the same filters and comparisons as the rest of Reports.
takeaways: Events report: confirm your events arrive; Pages: page titles vs paths matter
Landing page shows where visits begin; (not set) means no page view started the session
Retention needs weeks of data; age, gender and interests need Google signals

quiz.q: Two different URLs share the title 'Product' and appear as one row. Which change separates them?
options: Switch the primary dimension to Page path and screen class
Mark page_view as a key event
quiz.explain: The default first column is the page title; the page path dimension tells the URLs apart.

concepts.name: Customising reports in the Library
concepts.summary: Edit report cards, dimensions and metrics, build new detail reports and organise collections in the Library.
concepts.why: The default reports rarely match your **KPIs** (key performance indicators: the few numbers your business is judged by); editors can reshape them without touching Explore.
concepts.body:
Users with the *Editor* or *Administrator* role can change what the Reports section contains. Two places:

**Customise a report** (pencil icon, top right of any report). For a detail report you can change the primary and secondary dimension lists, add or remove metrics, choose chart types, add a permanent **report filter** (for example, exclude `hostname = staging.example.com`) and reorder cards. *Save* either overwrites the current report or saves a copy. For overview reports you pick which summary cards appear.

**Library** (bottom of the Reports nav) is where collections are managed. A **collection** is a group of **topics**, each a group of reports. You can:

- create a new detail report from scratch (*Create new report*): choose dimensions, metrics, charts and filters,
- create a new overview report by assembling cards from existing reports,
- create a collection, arrange topics and reports in it, and **publish** it so it appears in the left nav for everyone on the property,
- unpublish or hide the default collections if the business-objective layout fits your team better.

Some linked data only appears once you publish its collection: the *Search Console* collection stays in the Library until you add it.

Limits: a property can hold up to 150 custom detail reports and a handful of custom collections; reports are property-wide, so one person's edit changes what everyone sees. That is both the point and the risk: agree on an owner.

When a question needs more than dimensions, metrics and one filter (such as segments, funnels, or rows beyond the top 250, all covered in the Explore lessons), move to Explore.
takeaways: Pencil icon customises a report; Library manages collections and new reports
Published collections appear for everyone on the property
Permanent filters live in custom reports; for segments and funnels go to Explore

quiz.q: Who sees a custom collection after you publish it?
options: Only users with the Editor role
Everyone with access to the property
quiz.explain: Reports and collections are property assets, not personal ones.

concepts.name: What explorations are
concepts.summary: Explore works on individual events with segments, funnels and paths; it may estimate from a sample, and only sees recent data.
concepts.why: Knowing when a question belongs in Explore rather than Reports saves time and avoids misreading estimated numbers.
concepts.body:
**Explore** (in the left menu) is GA4's workspace for one-off analysis. Standard reports read from totals GA4 worked out in advance; an **exploration** goes back to the individual events (the **raw event data**) each time you change it. That gives you things reports can't:

- any combination of dimensions and metrics, including rows within rows, and dimensions turned into columns,
- **segments** (chosen groups of users, sessions or events) and conditions about the order things happened in,
- views beyond tables, such as step-by-step funnels, the paths users took, and one user's full timeline,
- tables with up to 500 rows and export to Sheets, CSV or PDF.

The trade-offs are just as important:

- **Retention window**: explorations can only see events within your **data retention** setting, which says how long GA4 keeps individual events (2 or 14 months, up to 50 for 360). A standard report happily shows three years; an exploration over the same range silently returns nothing older than the window.
- **Sampling**: when one exploration has to read more than 10 million events (1 billion for 360), GA4 reads only part of them, a sample, and scales the result up. An icon at the top right of each tab shows a green tick for unsampled data or a warning with the sampling percentage.
- **Thresholding** (hiding rows with very few people) applies as in reports, and new data takes as long to arrive (typically a few hours to a day).
- Explorations are personal: created by you, visible only to you unless shared, and sharing is read-only. Each user can own up to 200 explorations per property, and a property holds up to 500 shared ones.

There are seven kinds of analysis, called **techniques**: tables and charts (Free form), funnels, paths, overlaps between segments, one user's full timeline, groups of users by start date, and lifetime totals per user. The coming lessons cover each. One exploration can hold up to ten tabs mixing them, all drawing on the same list of dimensions and metrics.

Rule of thumb: Reports for keeping an eye on the numbers you track every week; Explore for a question you have not answered before.
takeaways: Explore works on individual events: segments, funnels, paths, cohorts, 500-row tables
Limits: retention window, sampling (estimates) above 10M events, thresholding
Explorations are personal; sharing is read-only; 200 per user, 500 shared per property

quiz.q: Your retention is 2 months. An exploration with a 6-month date range shows...
options: Only the last two months of data
quiz.explain: Explorations never see events older than the retention setting; reports do.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an Explore technique?
quiz.explain: Attribution lives in the Advertising section; the seven techniques are free form, funnel, path, overlap, user explorer, cohort and lifetime.

concepts.name: The Explore workspace
concepts.summary: Variables, Tab settings and the canvas: how the three panels of an exploration fit together.
concepts.why: Every technique uses the same layout, so once you can drive one, you can drive them all.
concepts.body:
Open Explore and pick *Blank* (or a template such as *Funnel exploration* or *Free form*). The screen has three panels.

**Variables** (left) is the shopping list for the whole exploration: a name, the **date range**, and the **segments**, **dimensions** and **metrics** you have imported. Click the `+` next to each to open a picker and tick what you need; up to 20 dimensions and 20 metrics per exploration. Nothing you add here shows up yet; it just becomes available to tabs.

**Tab settings** (middle) configures the current tab: the **technique** (the kind of analysis, such as a table or a funnel), the visualisation (table or chart type), and the slots that technique offers. For a free-form table the slots are *Rows*, *Columns*, *Values* (metrics) and *Filters*; a funnel has *Steps* and *Breakdown*; a path has *Starting point* and *Node type* (later lessons cover both). You fill slots by dragging from Variables or by clicking a slot and choosing. Segments dropped here apply only to this tab, so you can compare the same table with and without a segment on two tabs.

**Canvas** (right) renders the result and updates as you change settings. Right-click a row, bar or node for actions: *Include only* / *Exclude* (creates a tab filter), *Create segment from selection*, *View users* (opens User explorer for those users).

Tabs sit across the top; duplicate a tab to branch off an analysis and keep the original. Everything auto-saves; there is no save button. Renaming the exploration and its tabs is worth the five seconds when you have twenty of them.

The icon showing sampling and thresholding sits at the top right of the canvas; check it before quoting a number.

The *Share* icon makes the exploration visible read-only to others on the property; they can *Duplicate* to get an editable copy. *Export* gives Google Sheets, CSV or PDF files.
takeaways: Variables = what is available; Tab settings = how this tab uses it; Canvas = result
Segments applied in Tab settings affect only that tab
Right-click the canvas to filter, segment or view users; everything auto-saves

quiz.q: You added 'Country' in Variables but the table does not change. Why?
options: Country is not available in Explore
Variables only make a dimension available; it must be placed in Rows or Columns in Tab settings
Country only works as a segment
quiz.explain: The Variables panel is a palette; Tab settings decide what the current tab shows.

concepts.name: Free-form tables
concepts.summary: Build a table with rows, columns and values, nest rows, pivot and filter: the workhorse of Explore.
concepts.why: Most analysis questions are a table; free form gives you full control over its shape.
concepts.body:
The **Free form** technique with the *Table* visualisation is where you will spend most Explore time. Tab settings slots:

- **Rows**: up to five dimensions. With more than one, they nest: *Country* then *Device category* gives a row per combination. The **Nested rows** toggle shows them as an indented tree instead of a flat list. *Start row* and *Show rows* (10 to 500) page through long lists.
- **Columns**: up to two dimensions pivoted across the top, e.g. *Month* to turn a list into a trend table or *Session default channel group* to compare channels side by side. *Show columns* limits how many values.
- **Values**: up to ten metrics. **Cell type** can be plain numbers, a small bar chart in each cell, or a **heat map**, which colours cells by size so unusually high or low values stand out without reading the numbers.
- **Filters**: up to ten conditions on dimensions or metrics (*Page path contains /blog/*, *Event count > 100*). Filters restrict the rows of this tab; they are not segments.
- **Segment comparisons**: up to four segments; the table then shows one block per segment.

A useful recipe: Rows = *Landing page + query string*, Columns = *Session default channel group*, Values = *Sessions*, *Engagement rate*, *Key events*, filter *Sessions > 50*. Sort by clicking a metric header.

Moving a dimension from Rows to Columns is called **pivoting** it, and the canvas updates immediately.

Remember scopes: a table with *Session source* in rows and *Users* in values asks how many users had at least one session from each source, which double-counts users across rows. That is expected, not an error; the totals at the bottom count each user once.

Right-click any cell to drill: *Include only*, *Exclude*, *Create segment from selection*, *View users*.
takeaways: Rows (up to 5, nestable), Columns (up to 2), Values (up to 10), Filters (up to 10)
Cell type bar/heat map makes patterns visible; Show rows goes to 500
Users can be counted in several rows; the total at the bottom counts each user once

quiz.q: You want a row per landing page and a column per month. Where does Month go?
quiz.explain: Columns pivot a dimension across the top; Rows would instead nest months under pages.

concepts.name: Free-form charts and anomaly detection
concepts.summary: Switch a free-form tab to donut, line, scatter, bar or geo, and turn on anomaly detection on a line chart.
concepts.why: A chart answers 'is it changing?' and 'is it unusual?' faster than a table.
concepts.body:
The Free form technique has six **visualisations**; all read the same Rows/Values slots, so you can try things out in a table and then flip to a chart.

- **Donut chart**: share of one metric across one dimension; the breakdown dimension is the first row dimension. Good for channel mix or device share, limited to a handful of slices with *Other*.
- **Line chart**: a metric over time. Granularity (the time step) is day, week or month; the breakdown dimension (optional) draws one line per value, capped at a few top values. This is the only visualisation with **Anomaly detection**: tick it in Tab settings, set a *training period* (how many prior days to learn from, 7 to 90) and *sensitivity* (the probability threshold). GA4 predicts a likely range for each point from the training period; points outside that range are circled, which is exactly the signal behind the Insights cards in Reports, now under your control.
- **Scatter plot**: two metrics as x and y, one point per dimension value, optionally a third metric as bubble size. Use it to find pages with high views but low engagement, or campaigns with high cost but few key events.
- **Bar chart**: horizontal bars for one metric across one dimension, with an optional breakdown.
- **Geo map**: a metric by *Country*, *Region* or *City* on a world map.

Line and bar charts honour segments as separate series, so applying two segments gives a direct visual comparison.

Two surprises. First, charts use the same date range as the tab, and the line chart's granularity cannot exceed what the range allows. Second, `(not set)` and `(other)` rows appear in charts too; add a filter to drop them before presenting.

Export a chart as PDF, or screenshot it; charts do not export to Sheets, only tables do.
takeaways: Six visualisations share the same Rows/Values settings
Anomaly detection lives on the line chart: training period and sensitivity
Scatter plots compare two metrics per dimension value to find outliers

quiz.q: Which visualisation lets you flag unusual daily values automatically?
quiz.explain: Anomaly detection is a line-chart option that forecasts from a training period and marks outliers.

concepts.name: Funnel exploration
concepts.summary: Define ordered steps and see how many users complete each one, where they drop off, and how long it took.
concepts.why: Drop-off between steps is the number in product analytics you can most often act on.
concepts.body:
A **funnel** is a series of steps you expect users to take, which fewer and fewer people complete, like sand through a funnel. **Funnel exploration** answers "of the users who did A, how many went on to do B and C?". In Tab settings:

- **Steps** (up to ten): each step is a condition on an event, a dimension or a metric, e.g. *Event name = view_item*, then *add_to_cart*, then *begin_checkout*, then *purchase*. A step can have several conditions (*page_location contains /pricing* AND *device category = mobile*). Between steps you can choose *is directly followed by* (the next event the user fired) or *is indirectly followed by* (anything can happen in between, the default), and add a **within** time constraint (within 10 minutes, within 2 days).
- **Visualisation**: *Standard funnel* (bars with completion rate and abandonment per step) or **Trended funnel** (a line per step over time, so you can see whether a release moved step 3's completion).
- **Make open funnel**: see the next lesson.
- **Breakdown**: one dimension (device category, country, first user source) splitting every step into up to 15 rows.
- **Show elapsed time**: adds the average time users took between consecutive steps.
- **Next action**: shows the top five events (or page titles) users fired right after each step, which tells you where the drop-offs went instead.
- **Segments** (up to four) to compare, say, new vs returning users as separate funnels.

The canvas shows, per step, *Users* and *Completion rate*, plus *Abandonments* and *Abandonment rate* (the share who didn't continue) between steps. Funnels are user-based: a user who did step 2 before step 1 within the date range does not count as completing step 2.

Funnels are retroactive. Unlike Universal Analytics goal funnels, you can define a new funnel today and see last month's data, within the retention window.

Right-click a step to create a segment of users who dropped off there and send them to User explorer or build an audience from them.
takeaways: Steps are ordered event/dimension conditions; users must do them in order
Directly vs indirectly followed, time constraints, breakdown, elapsed time, next action
Retroactive within the retention window, unlike UA goal funnels

quiz.q: Step 2 is 'is directly followed by' step 3. A user fires step 2, then a scroll event, then step 3. Counted?
options: No; a different event came in between
quiz.explain: Directly followed means the very next event must match step 3; use indirectly followed to allow other events.

concepts.name: Open vs closed funnels and funnel diagnostics
concepts.summary: Choose between open and closed funnels, and use breakdown, elapsed time, next action and trends to diagnose a leak.
concepts.why: Open vs closed changes the numbers dramatically, and the diagnostic options turn a chart into a to-do list.
concepts.body:
A **closed funnel** (the default) only counts users who entered at step 1. Someone who landed directly on the checkout page is excluded, and the completion rates read as "of those who started here". It is right for designed flows such as onboarding or checkout, and for asking how good the flow is.

An **open funnel** (*Make open funnel* toggle) lets users enter at any step. A user who skipped straight to step 3 is counted at steps 3 and 4. The numbers at later steps rise, often sharply, and the funnel now answers "how many people reached this point, however they got here". Use it for loosely ordered journeys, such as reading through articles, or when links and ads send people straight to a page in the middle of the flow.

When a step leaks, work through the diagnostics in order:

- **Breakdown** by *Device category* or *Browser*: a leak isolated to one platform is a bug, not a design problem.
- **Next action**: if users who abandoned checkout next fired `view_cart` or `page_view` of the shipping page, the price or a form is the issue; if they fired nothing, they left the site.
- **Elapsed time**: a step that takes users minutes instead of seconds is a confusing step.
- **Trended funnel**: did the drop appear on a specific date? Line that date up with site releases and campaign launches.
- **Segments**: compare new vs returning, or a segment of a campaign's users, as separate funnels.

Two accuracy notes. A funnel spanning sessions works because funnels are user-based, but a step condition on a session-scoped dimension (such as *Session source*) is evaluated per event's session, which can exclude users who switched sources. And funnel user counts respect the reporting identity: with User-ID, a user who added to cart on mobile and bought on desktop completes.

All funnel data is subject to the retention window and sampling like any exploration.
takeaways: Closed: must enter at step 1; open: any step; later steps grow in open funnels
Diagnose leaks with breakdown, next action, elapsed time and trended view
Funnels are user-based across sessions and devices (with User-ID)

quiz.q: Switching a checkout funnel from closed to open makes step 4 jump from 800 to 2,100 users. Why?
options: Users who entered the flow at a later step are now counted
Open funnels count sessions instead of users
quiz.explain: An open funnel admits users at any step, so people who skipped early steps add to later counts.

quiz.q: Which option tells you what abandoning users did instead?
quiz.explain: Next action lists the top events users fired right after each step, including after dropping off.

concepts.name: Segments and segment overlap
concepts.summary: Build subsets of users, sessions or events with scoped conditions, tell them apart from filters, and compare them with segment overlap.
concepts.why: Segments are how you ask 'how does this group behave?' and are the most powerful Explore feature.
concepts.body:
A **segment** is a subset of your data defined by conditions. Create one from the Variables panel (`+` next to Segments) or by right-clicking on the canvas. Besides suggested segments, custom ones come in three types:

- **User segment**: all events from users who match. *Users who purchased* includes their browsing from before the purchase.
- **Session segment**: all events from sessions that match. *Sessions from Paid Search* keeps those visits, not the same users' organic visits.
- **Event segment**: only the matching events, e.g. *purchase events with value > 100*.

Pick the scope by asking: everything about these people, everything in these visits, or only these events?

Conditions use dimensions and metrics with comparisons (equals, contains, matches a regular expression, which is a text pattern, greater than, is one of), grouped in *Include* and *Exclude* blocks with AND/OR. Each condition group has its own **scoping**: *Across all sessions* (default for user segments), *Within the same session* or *Within the same event*. "Viewed pricing AND purchased" means something different across all sessions than within one session.

A user segment has a **Build an audience** checkbox that creates a matching audience (a saved group of users that Google Ads can use; see the Audiences lesson); the reverse is impossible.

**Filters vs segments**: a tab filter removes rows from the output; a segment changes the population before metrics are computed, and only segments can express exclusions and sequences. A *user* segment of German users also brings their sessions from abroad; a filter *Country = DE* would not.

**Segment overlap** is the technique that draws up to three segments as overlapping circles (a Venn diagram), with a table of every combination and the metrics you choose. Use it to check whether two groups are really the same people (mobile users vs purchasers). Right-click a region and choose **Create segment from selection** to turn an intersection into a reusable segment. Users are counted even for session and event segments, so mixing scopes is legal but easy to misread.

Segments are retroactive, which audiences are not, and up to four apply per tab.
takeaways: User, session and event segments keep different sets of events
Condition scoping (across sessions / same session / same event) changes meaning
Filters trim output rows; segments redefine the population and support exclusions
Segment overlap compares up to three segments and spawns intersection segments

quiz.q: You build a session segment 'Session medium = email'. Which events does it include?
options: Every event in sessions that started from email
All events ever from users who had an email session
Only key events in those sessions
quiz.explain: Session scope keeps whole sessions that match; user scope would keep every session of those users.

quiz.q: In a segment overlap, the 'A and B' region is blank with a warning icon. Most likely reason?
options: Data thresholding hid a small group
quiz.explain: Small user groups are withheld when thresholding applies; switch to device-based identity to check.

concepts.name: Sequence segments
concepts.summary: Define users by an ordered series of steps, with direct or indirect succession and time limits.
concepts.why: Sequences express 'did A then B' questions that neither filters nor plain conditions can.
concepts.body:
A **sequence** is a user-segment condition that requires events in a particular order. In the segment builder choose *Add sequence* (available for user segments). Each **step** is a condition group like any other; between steps you choose *is indirectly followed by* (anything may happen in between) or *is directly followed by* (the very next event must match). Up to ten steps.

Options on the sequence:

- **Sequence scoping**: *Across all sessions* (steps may span visits) or *Within the same session*.
- **Time constraint**: the whole sequence must complete within N minutes, hours or days.
- *Step 1 must be the first event*: the first step has to be the user's first event in the date range, for "first thing they did" questions.

Examples of questions only sequences answer:

- Users who viewed a product then searched (they did not find what they wanted on the page).
- Users who started checkout and, within 30 minutes, viewed the shipping-policy page before purchasing.
- Users whose first event was a `page_view` of a blog post and who later signed up.

Sequences in segments complement funnels. A funnel shows counts per step for everyone; a sequence segment captures the people who completed (or failed) a path so you can look at anything else about them: their channels, their other pages, their lifetime value, their user explorer timelines. Combine both: build the funnel, then right-click a step to spawn a sequence segment of the users who reached it.

An **Exclude** block can also hold a sequence, which is how you express "users who added to cart but never purchased" cleanly: include *add_to_cart*, exclude a sequence or condition *purchase*. Exclusion can be *temporarily* (only events after the match are excluded) or *permanently* (the whole user is excluded).

Sequences are evaluated at query time over raw events, so they obey the retention window and can trigger sampling on big properties.
takeaways: Sequences require ordered steps; direct vs indirect succession and time limits
Scope across sessions or within one session; optional 'first event' anchor
Exclude blocks express 'did A but never B'

quiz.q: Which question needs a sequence rather than a plain AND condition?
options: Users who viewed /pricing and then signed up
quiz.explain: Order matters only in the second; the others are satisfied by unordered conditions or filters.

concepts.name: Path exploration
concepts.summary: Follow what users did before or after an event or page as a tree of nodes, forwards or backwards.
concepts.why: Paths reveal journeys you did not think to put in a funnel, including dead ends and loops.
concepts.body:
**Path exploration** draws a tree of boxes, called **nodes**: a starting node and, to its right, the most common next steps, each of which expands into its own next steps. Nodes can be one of three **node types**, chosen per column: *Event name*, *Page title and screen name* or *Page path and screen class*; you can mix them, say events for step 1 and page titles after.

Set a **starting point** (an event like `session_start` or a page) to ask "what happens next?". Or set an **ending point** instead to ask "how did people get here?"; GA4 then builds the tree backwards, which is the better question for a key event: what did purchasers do right before purchasing?

Each node shows the number of events (or users, switchable in Tab settings via *Node type* metrics) that flowed through it, with the top five branches shown and the rest in *+ more*. Click a node to expand it; the tree can grow very wide, so keep a breakdown dimension (*Device category*, *First user source*) in mind to colour nodes rather than adding columns.

Useful toggles:

- *View only unique nodes*: collapses repeated consecutive events such as `scroll, scroll, scroll`.
- Right-click a node to *Create segment from selection* or *Exclude* it; excluding noisy events like `user_engagement` and `scroll` from the node list makes paths readable. Do this early.
- A segment applied to the tab restricts whose paths are drawn.

Paths cross sessions unless you start from `session_start`. The technique is good at spotting loops (A to B back to A), unexpected exits to the help centre, and the pages that precede a conversion. It is bad at quantifying a long flow; build a funnel for that once a path has shown you which flow to measure.
takeaways: Start from an event/page to look forwards, or set an ending point to look backwards
Node types: event name, page title, page path; mixable per column
Exclude noisy events (scroll, user_engagement) first

quiz.q: You want to know which pages people viewed just before purchasing. Which setup?
options: Ending point = purchase, node type = page path
quiz.explain: An ending point builds the tree backwards from the chosen event.

concepts.name: User explorer
concepts.summary: Inspect individual users' event timelines and delete a single user's data from there.
concepts.why: Seeing one real journey end to end is the fastest way to validate a tagging plan or understand a drop-off.
concepts.body:
**User explorer** lists individual users (identified by the *App-instance ID* / client ID or your *User-ID*, shown as the *effective user ID*) with summary metrics: event count, sessions, engagement time, key events, revenue, first and last seen. Sort by any column, apply a segment to narrow the list, or arrive here by right-clicking users in another technique and choosing *View users*.

Click a row to open the **user activity** view: a vertical timeline of every event that user fired within the retention window, grouped by session, with the user's properties and acquisition details in a side card. Each event expands to show its parameters. Tick the event types you care about to declutter.

What it is good for:

- Checking your setup (QA): find your own test user (use DebugView to learn your client ID) and check the sequence of events, parameter values and session boundaries after a release.
- Understanding a funnel drop-off: open five users who abandoned step 3 and read what they actually did.
- Support investigations when a customer reports a problem and you have their User-ID.

What it is not for: reporting. The list is capped and sampled like any exploration, and users appear only as random IDs, not names (**pseudonymous**). Do not try to build counts from it.

In the user activity view the trash icon **deletes this user's data** from the property (a per-user deletion request, processed within about 72 hours). Bulk deletion by dimension values is in Admin > Data deletion requests. There is also a per-user export in the side card, which is one way to answer a person's request to see the data you hold about them, if you know their User-ID.

User explorer honours reporting identity: under Blended, a User-ID user shows all their devices in one timeline.
takeaways: A list of users known only by IDs with a per-user event timeline
Use it for QA, drop-off forensics and support, not for counts
Trash icon deletes one user's data; bulk deletion lives in Admin

quiz.q: Which is the right tool to see every event a specific logged-in customer fired last week?
options: User explorer with a segment on their User-ID
quiz.explain: User explorer shows the per-user timeline; a segment or sort on the effective user ID finds the person.

concepts.name: Cohort and user lifetime explorations
concepts.summary: Group users by when they arrived or acted and measure their return, plus per-user lifetime value and engagement.
concepts.why: Retention and lifetime value show whether you are really growing, or losing customers as fast as you gain them.
concepts.body:
A **cohort** is a group of users who started at the same time, such as everyone who first visited in the same week. **Cohort exploration** shows what share of each cohort came back in later periods, as a triangle-shaped table.

- **Inclusion criteria**: what puts a user in a cohort. *First touch (acquisition date)* is the classic new-user cohort; *Any event*, *Any transaction*, *Any key event* or a specific event also work, so you can cohort by "first purchase".
- **Return criteria**: what counts as coming back: *Any event* (just showed up), *Any transaction*, *Any key event* or a specific event.
- **Cohort granularity**: daily, weekly or monthly; the table shows up to 60 cohorts.
- **Calculation**: *Standard* (returned in that exact period), *Rolling* (returned in that period and every period before), *Cumulative* (returned in that period or any earlier one).
